templates.name: Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In addition to + -ing), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is a possessive noun phrase built on the obvious noun
items.passage: Elephants can coordinate their movements with members of their herd that are several kilometers away and out of sight. In addition to traveling through the air, ______ which other elephants appear to detect through sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: elephants send their low-pitched rumbles through the ground as vibrations,
elephants’ low-pitched rumbles pass through the ground as vibrations,
the passage of elephants’ low-pitched rumbles through the ground creates vibrations,
there are low-pitched rumbles from elephants that pass through the ground as vibrations,
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that travels through the air. Choice B places “elephants’ low-pitched rumbles” right after the phrase, making clear that the rumbles, not the elephants themselves, travel through the air and also pass through the ground as vibrations.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun
A.why_wrong: “Elephants” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the elephants themselves travel through the air.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the passage,” so the sentence illogically says that a passage travels through the air.

D.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there are,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (elephants send low-frequency rumbles through the ground as seismic vibrations that other elephants sense through their feet; no researchers named). Band-7 moves from spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md section 3 (7) and section 5: the opener describes a property of the animal, so the right subject is the possessive noun phrase “elephants’ low-pitched rumbles” and the obvious noun, “elephants” (the topic of sentence 1, which never mentions rumbles), is the trap (W). Recipes W, N, E, as in 37e5c794 (E, W, P) and 2dd1b8bf. Mid-sentence blank: each option ends in “vibrations,” and joins the relative clause after it. Each option read in the full sentence: only B leaves no dangling modifier.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: Move 7: the opener describes a property, so the right subject is the possessive phrase “elephants’ low-pitched rumbles” built on the obvious noun; the trap A keeps every fact with “elephants” as subject (W), as in 2dd1b8bf and 37e5c794; mid-sentence blank with 14 words after it, run about 32 words.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final blank; the right subject is the work (possessive noun phrase), not the artist
items.passage: Senegalese artist Ousmane Sow practiced physical therapy for some twenty years before devoting himself to sculpture in the 1980s. Standing far taller than a person and depicting wrestlers, warriors, and herders from several African peoples, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Sow drew some three million visitors when he displayed his figures on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
some three million visitors came to see Sow’s figures when they were displayed on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
Sow’s figures drew some three million visitors when they were displayed on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
there were some three million visitors to Sow’s figures when they were displayed on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes things that stand far taller than a person and depict wrestlers, warriors, and herders. Choice C places “Sow’s figures” right after the phrase, making clear that the sculptures, not the artist or the visitors, are what the phrase describes.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun
A.why_wrong: “Sow” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the artist himself stood far taller than a person.

B.why_wrong: “Some three million visitors” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the visitors stood far taller than a person and depicted wrestlers and warriors.

D.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there were,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Ousmane Sow, Senegalese sculptor and former physical therapist; his larger-than-life figures shown on the Pont des Arts in Paris in 1999 drew about three million visitors; known, real). Band-7 moves: the right subject is the possessive noun phrase “Sow’s figures” built on the obvious noun, the artist, who is the trap (W); “depicting” could describe an artist, so only “Standing far taller than a person” rules Sow out, a two-part check. Passage-final, as 2bca654a and dab8b8ee; recipes W, W, E (reviewer replaced the nominalised “the display of Sow’s figures,” since an exhibit can itself stand tall and depict figures). Options 15 to 19 words, all carrying the same facts.

fixes: D: replaced “the display of Sow’s figures ...” (a display can stand tall and depict, so defensible) with an expletive “there were ...” option
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: Move 7: the right subject “Sow’s figures” is built on the obvious noun, the artist; “depicting” fits Sow, so only “Standing far taller than a person” rules A out; sentence-final blank like its band-7 model 2bca654a; options carry the same facts. Weak D (a display can stand tall and depict) replaced by an expletive.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank; the right subject is the epic, not the historian or the readers
items.passage: For centuries, griots—hereditary oral historians and musicians of West Africa—have preserved the story of Sundiata Keita, the thirteenth-century founder of the Mali Empire. A narrative of exile, return, and military conquest, ______ in 1960, when it appeared in a French prose adaptation based on the recitation of a Guinean griot.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the epic of Sundiata reached a wide audience of readers
historian Djibril Tamsir Niane brought the epic of Sundiata to many readers
a wide audience of readers first encountered the epic of Sundiata
there was a wide audience of readers for the epic of Sundiata
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a story: a narrative of exile, return, and military conquest. Choice A places “the epic of Sundiata” right after the phrase, making clear that the epic is the narrative the phrase describes.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): a person
B.why_wrong: “Historian Djibril Tamsir Niane” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the historian is a narrative of exile, return, and military conquest.

C.why_wrong: “A wide audience of readers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the readers are a narrative of exile, return, and military conquest.

D.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there was,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: literature (the Sundiata epic of the griots, put into French prose by D. T. Niane in 1960 from the recitation of a Guinean griot, Mamadou Kouyaté; real, known). R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), and the plan sets band 6: a strong band 6. Mid-sentence blank like 5b8f9cf2 and e060dd6b: options end so the clause continues with “in 1960, when it appeared ...”. Recipes W (person), W (readers), E. Each option read in the full sentence; only A leaves no dangling modifier.

fixes: D: replaced the it-cleft (“it” could refer to “the story of Sundiata Keita,” a narrative, so defensible) with an expletive “there was ...” option
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; it is a strong band 6 on 5b8f9cf2 and e060dd6b (mid-sentence blank, three W/E distractors that keep every fact).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, plural head behind singular nouns and a relative clause with its own singular verb
items.passage: In 2007, Twyfelfontein, a valley in northwestern Namibia, became the country’s first UNESCO World Heritage Site. The petroglyphs at this site, whose concentration of rock art is among the highest in Africa, ______ attributed primarily to San hunter-gatherers, who engraved images of giraffes, rhinoceroses, and other animals into the sandstone over several millennia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The plural verb “are” agrees in number with the plural subject “The petroglyphs.” The words between the subject and the blank (“at this site, whose concentration of rock art is among the highest in Africa”) contain only singular nouns and a singular verb, but they do not change the number of the subject.

A.recipe: wrong number (singular present), agrees with the nearest nouns
A.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “The petroglyphs”; it matches “concentration” and “Africa” instead.

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “The petroglyphs.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “The petroglyphs.”

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (the rock engravings of Twyfelfontein, Namibia, inscribed by UNESCO in 2007 as Namibia’s first World Heritage Site, attributed mainly to San hunter-gatherers; real, known). Band-7 settings (section 5): plural head (as dc645172) behind singular nouns (site, concentration, rock art, Africa) and a relative clause whose own singular verb “is” makes the singular sound right twice; 20 run words after the blank; run 37 words. Be-family options, all three distractors singular.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: Plural head “petroglyphs” behind four singular nouns (site, concentration, rock art, Africa) and an intervener with its own singular verb “is” (moves 4 and 5, as dc645172); 20 words after the blank, run about 37; options are the wrong number in three tenses.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, missing main verb (passive) after an appositive holding two relative clauses with their own finite verbs
items.passage: Miura-ori, a tessellated folding pattern that Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura developed in the 1970s and that allows a flat membrane to collapse into a compact stack and then expand in a single continuous motion, ______ to package the solar array of the Space Flyer Unit, an experimental satellite that Japan launched in 1995.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Miura-ori” needs a finite main verb, but the long appositive after it, which describes the pattern, contains only the verbs of its two relative clauses (“developed” and “allows”). Choice C supplies the finite verb “was used,” completing the main clause: Miura-ori was used to package the solar array.

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: “Being used” is a nonfinite form, so the sentence would have no main verb.

B.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: “Having been used” is a nonfinite form, so the sentence would have no main verb.

D.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: “To be used” is a nonfinite form, so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: science and engineering (Miura-ori, the fold Koryo Miura devised, used for the 2D solar array of Japan’s Space Flyer Unit, launched 1995; real, known). The plan set band 7, but R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), so this is a strong band 6 with band_target 6, as w1b4_05, w2b2_05, w2b5_04 and w3b1_06 were. Frame varied from theirs (relative clauses, what-clause, dash pairs): an appositive holding two relative clauses with their own finite verbs (developed, allows), 33 words between the subject and the blank, as a75d5984 hides its subject behind a dash list. Passive key, as 1.35; no -ed distractor, so no reduced-relative reading.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 like a75d5984: subject head 35 words before the blank across two stacked relative clauses.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, “each one of” + plural noun + relative clause with its own plural verb
items.passage: Hawaiian kinship terminology classifies relatives by generation and gender rather than by lineage. Consequently, each one of a speaker’s aunts, who in English are distinguished from the mother by a separate term, ______ referred to by the same term as the speaker’s mother, makuahine, regardless of whether she is related through the maternal or the paternal line.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The singular verb “is” agrees in number with the singular subject “each one.” The phrase “of a speaker’s aunts” and the clause “who in English are distinguished from the mother by a separate term” contain a plural noun and a plural verb, but the head of the subject is “each one,” so each individual aunt is called by the same term as the mother.

B.recipe: wrong number (plural present), agrees with the plural noun and the clause’s own verb
B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each one”; it matches “aunts” instead.

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each one.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each one.”

items.notes: Subject: social science, anthropology and linguistics (Hawaiian kinship terminology: aunts on either side are called makuahine, the word for mother; real, well documented; no researchers named). Band-7 settings from 0fe5ce68 and 5fd86f4b: “each one of” + plural noun + a relative clause whose own plural verb (“are distinguished”) agrees with the attractor, so the plural sounds right twice; 24 run words after the blank; run 43 words. Architecture differs from w1b4_06 (compound with relative clauses) and w2b5_06 (X and Y, not Z). Be-family options as 5fd86f4b, all distractors plural.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: “each one of a speaker’s aunts, who ... are distinguished” puts a plural attractor and an intervener verb of the other number between head and blank (move 4, as 0fe5ce68 and 5fd86f4b); 25 words after the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, singular head + appositive containing a plural noun
items.passage: Isolated from the ocean at low tide, reef pools can become severely depleted of oxygen. The epaulette shark, a small predator inhabiting the shallow waters off northern Australia and New Guinea, ______ such hypoxic conditions remarkably well and can even use its paired fins to walk between pools.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The singular verb “tolerates” agrees in number with the singular subject “The epaulette shark.” The appositive between the subject and the blank contains the plural noun “waters,” but it does not change the number of the subject.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “tolerate” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “The epaulette shark.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are tolerating” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “The epaulette shark.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have tolerated” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “The epaulette shark.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (the epaulette shark of northern Australia and New Guinea tolerates low oxygen in tide pools and walks on its fins; no researchers named). Medium: a 13-word appositive with one plural attractor (waters), as 2.22 and 2.21; the plural “reef pools” in sentence 1 adds a second pull. Lexical family: V-s key, V, are V-ing, have V-ed.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: plural possessor + plural noun, two slots
items.passage: In the late 1930s, South African painter Gerard Sekoto lived in Sophiatown, a densely populated, culturally vibrant neighborhood of Johannesburg. His paintings from this period document the ______ from women hanging laundry in cramped backyards to musicians performing on crowded street corners.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The paintings show many people of the neighborhood, so the plural possessive “residents’” is needed to show that the routines belong to the residents. The plural noun “routines” takes no apostrophe because nothing belongs to the routines.

A.recipe: wrong possessor number + needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Resident’s” refers to a single resident, but the paintings show many people, and “routine’s” wrongly adds an apostrophe to a plural noun that possesses nothing.

C.why_wrong: “Residents” lacks the apostrophe needed to show that the routines belong to the residents.

D.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
D.why_wrong: “Routine’s” wrongly uses an apostrophe; the routines don’t possess anything, so the plain plural “routines” is needed.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Gerard Sekoto’s paintings of Sophiatown, Johannesburg, late 1930s; real, known). Two-slot grid as 2.5 and 2.24, but with a plural possessor: the cue for plural “residents’” is the densely populated neighborhood and the women and musicians listed after the blank, who also make “routines” plural. Distractors cover the three R6 recipes (wrong possessor number, missing apostrophe, needless apostrophe). Options carry the trailing comma, as 2.14 carries its period.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By + -ing), mid-sentence blank; plain agent key
items.passage: In the sixth century BCE, engineer Eupalinos of Megara designed an aqueduct tunnel to carry water through a mountain to the ancient Greek city of Samos. By excavating from both ends simultaneously, ______ through more than a kilometer of solid rock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: two teams of workers cut the channel
the channel was cut by two teams of workers
there were two teams of workers who cut the channel
the cutting of the channel by two teams of workers went
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes people who excavated from both ends simultaneously. Choice A places “two teams of workers” right after the phrase, making clear that the workers did the excavating.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “The channel” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the channel excavated from both ends.

C.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there were,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the cutting,” so the sentence illogically says that the cutting excavated from both ends.

items.notes: Subject: history and engineering (the Tunnel of Eupalinos on Samos, sixth century BCE, about 1 kilometer long and dug from both ends; real, well known to historians, not a viral subject). Medium as 2.17 and 2.2: a short, clear opener, mid-sentence blank, plain agent key. Recipes V, E, N; Eupalinos himself is kept out of the options because an engineer can loosely be said to dig a tunnel.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, singular head + of-phrase with a plural noun right before the blank
items.passage: A spilled drop of coffee usually dries into a dark ring because liquid flowing toward its edge carries suspended particles there. In 2011, however, physicists showed that the shape of those particles ______ crucial: stretched, oval particles deform the drop’s surface and spread out evenly instead of collecting at the rim.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The singular verb “is” agrees in number with the singular subject “the shape.” The prepositional phrase “of those particles” contains a plural noun, but the head of the subject is “shape.”

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present), agrees with the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “the shape”; it matches “particles” instead.

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “the shape.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “the shape.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, physics (the coffee-ring stain and the 2011 finding that elongated, ellipsoidal particles suppress it; no researchers named). Medium: the plural attractor “particles” sits right before the blank, and the passage is full of plurals (particles twice more). Be-family options; “was” is not offered, so tense never decides.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Tense, simple past with a dated cue after the blank and present-tense framing before it
items.passage: Ethiopian empress Taytu Betul is widely credited with establishing Addis Ababa. Historians note that Taytu, attracted by the area’s hot springs, ______ the location for a royal residence in 1886, and the settlement that developed around it soon replaced the mountaintop town of Entoto as the imperial capital.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes a completed action at a specific time in the past, “in 1886,” and the parallel verb “replaced” is also in the simple past. The simple past “chose” fits that time frame.

A.recipe: present perfect where a dated past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present perfect “has chosen” can’t be used with a specific past date such as “in 1886.”

B.why_wrong: The future “will choose” describes an action that hasn’t happened yet, but the choice was made in 1886.

C.why_wrong: The present progressive “is choosing” describes an action happening now, but the choice was made in 1886.

items.notes: Subject: history (Taytu Betul chose the site of Addis Ababa near the Filwoha hot springs in 1886; the court soon moved down from Entoto; real, known). Medium as 2.12: present-tense framing (“is widely credited,” “Historians note”) tempts a present or present perfect form, and the date sits after the blank. Distractor recipes as 2.12 (present perfect, progressive, future); “chooses” not offered.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, second verb of a compound predicate split by a dash pair
items.passage: Japanese jazz pianist Toshiko Akiyoshi relocated to the United States in 1956 to study music in Boston. In 1973, she established a big band with saxophonist Lew Tabackin—her husband and the ensemble’s principal soloist—and ______ most of its repertoire, integrating elements of traditional Japanese music into big band jazz.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank holds the second verb of a compound predicate: she “established” a big band “and” composed most of its repertoire. The finite past-tense verb “composed” matches “established.” The dash pair only interrupts the predicate.

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The nonfinite “composing” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “established”; a finite past-tense verb is needed.

C.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to compose” can’t serve as the second verb of the predicate that begins with “established.”

D.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite “having composed” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “established.”

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (Toshiko Akiyoshi, Japanese jazz pianist, at Berklee from 1956; her big band, formed in Los Angeles in 1973 with Lew Tabackin, played mostly her own compositions with Japanese elements; real, known). Medium as 2.1 (b74f676f): a dash pair splits the compound predicate, so “established” is out of sight when the blank arrives.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Tense, present habitual (seasonal cue and parallel present verbs)
items.passage: In Cambodia, the Tonle Sap River ordinarily drains Tonle Sap, the largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia, into the Mekong River. During the monsoon season, however, the swollen Mekong forces water back upstream, and the Tonle Sap River ______ direction, flowing into the lake instead.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes something that happens regularly, every monsoon season, and uses present-tense verbs such as “drains” and “forces.” The simple present “reverses” fits this habitual, present time frame.

B.recipe: simple past where a habitual present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past tense “reversed” describes a single event in the past, but the passage describes something that happens every monsoon season.

C.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
C.why_wrong: The past perfect “had reversed” refers to an action completed before another past action, which doesn’t fit the present-tense description.

D.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have reversed” refers to an action completed by a future time, which doesn’t fit the present-tense description.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, hydrology (the Tonle Sap River in Cambodia reverses its flow each wet season when the Mekong rises; real, known). Easy as 1.17 and 1.37: a habitual cue (“During the monsoon season”) and present verbs (“ordinarily drains,” “forces”) in the same passage.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement, subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: Congolese painter Chéri Samba began his career in Kinshasa, producing signs and billboards for local businesses. In 1975, ______ opened his own studio, where he developed his signature style: brightly colored scenes accompanied by blocks of handwritten commentary, much like the speech balloons in comic strips.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the painter, Chéri Samba, who is one person. The singular pronoun “he” agrees in number with this antecedent and with “his own studio.”

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent, the painter Chéri Samba.

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent and doesn’t clearly refer to Samba.

D.why_wrong: The pronoun “both” refers to two people, but only one person, Samba, opened the studio.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Chéri Samba, Congolese painter, began as a sign and billboard painter in Kinshasa and opened his own studio in 1975; his paintings carry handwritten text; real, known). Easy as 1.33: the antecedent is the named person, with options from the 1.33 set (plural personal, demonstrative, indefinite).

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement, subject pronoun for a singular thing (a study)
items.passage: Japanese botanist Kono Yasui devoted her career to investigating the cellular structure of plants. In 1911, she published a detailed study of the life cycle of the aquatic fern Salvinia natans in the British journal Annals of Botany. ______ was the first article by a Japanese woman to appear in an international scientific journal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the singular noun “study,” Yasui’s 1911 article. The singular pronoun “It” agrees in number with this antecedent and with the singular verb “was.”

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “They” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “study.”

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “Those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “study.”

C.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “These” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “study.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science and history of science (Kono Yasui’s 1911 paper on Salvinia natans in Annals of Botany, the first by a Japanese woman in a foreign journal; real, known). Easy as 1.39: a singular thing as antecedent, with the plural “plants” a sentence away. No singular demonstrative is offered, since “This” could defend itself for a specific paper.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, singular name + appositive
items.passage: Amanirenas, a queen who ruled the Nubian kingdom of Kush from its capital at Meroë, ______ a commander of the Kushite army during a prolonged war against the Roman Empire from about 25 to 21 BCE. Her troops captured several fortified towns in Roman Egypt before negotiations ended the conflict.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The singular verb “was” agrees in number with the singular subject “Amanirenas.” The appositive “a queen who ruled the Nubian kingdom of Kush from its capital at Meroë” describes her but doesn’t change the number of the subject.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Amanirenas.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Amanirenas.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Amanirenas.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Amanirenas, queen of Kush, led the Kushite war against Rome about 25 to 21 BCE; her forces took towns on Egypt’s southern frontier and a treaty ended the war; real, known). Easy as 1.4: a name, an appositive with no plural noun, and the blank.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, plural head + appositive, no number clash
items.passage: For centuries, Zuni farmers in what is now New Mexico have cultivated crops in waffle gardens. These gardens, small sunken plots divided into squares by low earthen walls, ______ scarce rainwater and shelter young plants from desiccating winds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The plural verb “trap” agrees in number with the plural subject “These gardens.” It also matches the plural verb “shelter” that follows.

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “traps” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “These gardens.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “is trapping” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “These gardens.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “has trapped” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “These gardens.”

items.notes: Subject: social science and agriculture (Zuni waffle gardens, sunken grid beds with earthen walls that hold water and break the wind; real, known). Easy: plural head and an appositive of plural and singular nouns with no number clash, as 1.7; the parallel “shelter” confirms the plural. Plural key, as 1.18 and 1.34.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, plural head + appositive with a relative clause
items.passage: Amur falcons, small birds of prey that nest in northeastern China and southeastern Siberia, ______ to southern Africa each autumn. Their annual round-trip journey can exceed 20,000 kilometers and includes a nonstop crossing of the Arabian Sea.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The plural verb “migrate” agrees in number with the plural subject “Amur falcons.” The appositive “small birds of prey that nest in northeastern China and southeastern Siberia” describes the falcons but doesn’t change the number of the subject.

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “migrates” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “Amur falcons.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “is migrating” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “Amur falcons.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has migrated” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “Amur falcons.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Amur falcon migration between eastern Asia and southern Africa, about 20,000 kilometers a year with a sea crossing over the Arabian Sea; real, known). Easy: an appositive of plural nouns, so no number clash, as 1.34 has none.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, missing main verb after a short subject
items.passage: Jellyfish Lake, on an island in the Pacific nation of Palau, is home to millions of golden jellyfish. Each day, the jellyfish ______ horizontally across the lake, tracking the Sun so that the photosynthetic algae living inside their tissues receive sufficient light.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “the jellyfish” needs a finite main verb. Choice C supplies the finite present-tense verb “migrate,” which completes the main clause.

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: “Migrating” is a nonfinite form, so the sentence would have no main verb.

B.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: “Having migrated” is a nonfinite form, so the sentence would have no main verb.

D.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: “To migrate” is a nonfinite form, so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (the golden jellyfish of Jellyfish Lake, Palau, follow the Sun across the lake each day for their symbiotic algae; real, known). Easy as 1.23 and 1.31: a bare main-verb slot after a short subject, canonical distractor set.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun, two slots
items.passage: Nigerian writer Cyprian Ekwensi’s 1954 novel People of the City follows Amusa Sango, a young crime reporter who also leads a popular dance band in Lagos. The ______ through the bustling, rapidly growing city reveal both its excitement and its many dangers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The wanderings belong to one character, Amusa Sango, so the singular possessive “character’s” is needed. The plural noun “wanderings,” which agrees with the plural verb “reveal,” takes no apostrophe because nothing belongs to the wanderings.

A.why_wrong: “Characters” lacks an apostrophe to show possession and wrongly refers to more than one character.

C.recipe: wrong possessor number + needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Characters’” refers to more than one character, but the novel follows one, and “wandering’s” wrongly adds an apostrophe to a noun that possesses nothing.

D.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
D.why_wrong: “Wandering’s” wrongly uses an apostrophe; the wanderings don’t possess anything, so the plain plural “wanderings” is needed.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Cyprian Ekwensi’s 1954 Lagos novel People of the City and its hero Amusa Sango, crime reporter and bandleader; real, known). Easy two-slot grid as 1.16: the single named character is the cue for “character’s,” and the plural verb “reveal” for “wanderings.”

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Tense, past perfect for an action earlier than a dated past event
items.passage: In 1924, Japanese inventor Sakichi Toyoda completed the Type G, an automatic loom that could replace an empty shuttle without interrupting production. Toyoda ______ his first loom, a manually operated wooden model, more than three decades earlier, in 1890.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first loom was built “more than three decades earlier” than the 1924 loom, so the action happened before another past action. The past perfect “had built” shows that order.

B.recipe: present simple where the past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: The present tense “builds” doesn’t fit an action completed in 1890.

C.why_wrong: The future tense “will build” describes an action that hasn’t happened yet, but the loom was built in 1890.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive “is building” describes an action happening now, but the loom was built in 1890.

items.notes: Subject: history of invention (Sakichi Toyoda’s wooden hand loom of 1890 and his Type G automatic loom of 1924; real, known). Easy as 1.24: an explicit “earlier” cue against a dated past event; verb changed from 1.24’s “invent” to keep the option set from cloning it.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: New York City is among the most linguistically diverse places on Earth, home to speakers of hundreds of languages, some rarely spoken elsewhere. In 2010, linguists and activists established the Endangered Language Alliance in the city ______ these languages and assist the communities that use them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “linguists and activists established the Endangered Language Alliance in the city” is already complete. The infinitive “to document” begins a phrase that gives the purpose of founding the organization, and it matches the parallel infinitive form “assist.”

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “documents” has no subject of its own here, so it can’t follow the complete clause.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “documented” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction or subject.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “is documenting” has no subject of its own here, so it can’t follow the complete clause.

items.notes: Subject: social science, linguistics (the Endangered Language Alliance, founded in New York City in 2010 to document the city’s minority and endangered languages; real, known; founders not named). Easy as 1.22: purpose infinitive after a complete clause, with three finite distractors.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, second verb of a compound predicate
items.passage: Cuban poet Nicolás Guillén published Motivos de son, a collection of eight short poems, in 1930. In these poems, Guillén reproduced the vernacular speech of working-class Black residents of Havana and ______ the syncopated rhythms of son, a popular Afro-Cuban musical genre.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank holds the second verb of a compound predicate: Guillén “reproduced” the speech of Havana’s residents “and” echoed the rhythms of son. The finite past-tense verb “echoed” matches “reproduced.”

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The nonfinite “echoing” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “reproduced.”

C.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to echo” can’t serve as the second verb of the predicate that begins with “reproduced.”

D.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite “having echoed” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “reproduced.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Nicolás Guillén’s Motivos de son, 1930, eight poems in Afro-Cuban vernacular modeled on son; real, known). Easy as 1.11: “reproduced ... and ______” with the canonical nonfinite distractors.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, -ing participial phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: Lugworms inhabit U-shaped burrows in the sandy shores and mudflats along the coasts of the North Atlantic. The worms continually ingest sediment and digest the bacteria and other microorganisms coating its grains, ______ distinctive coiled casts of processed sand at the surface beside each burrow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “The worms continually ingest sediment and digest the bacteria and other microorganisms coating its grains” is complete, so the blank must begin a phrase that describes a result. The participle “leaving” does this without creating a second independent clause.

A.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
A.why_wrong: “This leaves” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “leaves” has no subject of its own here and doesn’t agree with “The worms,” so it can’t follow the comma.

D.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
D.why_wrong: “They leave” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (lugworms of North Atlantic shores swallow sediment, digest the microorganisms on it and leave coiled casts; real, known). Easy as 1.29: a result phrase after a complete clause, with two comma-splice options and a bare finite form.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard
